key_claims: Routine assessment often misses the earliest signs of cognitive decline from mild cognitive impairment to dementia.
EEG markers and deep learning models report strong accuracy but many rely on small, single-site datasets unlikely to survive rigorous external validation.
Plasma p-tau217 has reached clinical utility, with the first blood test cleared to aid Alzheimer's diagnosis in 2025.
Anti-amyloid therapies (lecanemab, donanemab) are approved despite modest, contested benefits.
Wearable, remote, speech, and virtual-reality tools enable continuous, ecologically valid monitoring, and multimodal fusion improves sensitivity and specificity.
Barriers remain: standardization, explainability, data privacy, and equitable, externally validated deployment.
limitations: The source is an abstract and may not include full methodological details.
The source does not specify the number of studies reviewed or the criteria for inclusion.
The source does not provide quantitative effect sizes or confidence intervals for the reported findings.
The source does not detail the specific barriers or how they might be overcome.
what_not_to_say: The source does not claim that EEG or deep learning models are clinically validated or ready for widespread use.
The source does not claim that anti-amyloid therapies are definitively effective or safe.
The source does not claim that the blood test is universally available or recommended for all patients.
The source does not claim that wearable or remote monitoring tools are superior to traditional assessments in all settings.
